title: Gold Coast call centre at heart of super ‘health check’ scheme raking in millions
full_text:
The key players behind a lucrative superannuation scheme that scooped $10m a month in retirement savings from Aussie workers has been exposed, as a fresh wave of companies target Australia’s $4.5 trillion super pool.
Thousands of clients across Australia were drawn into superannuation switching schemes – including the now-collapsed Shield Master Fund and Global Capital Property Fund – with millions of dollars brought in from an unassuming Gold Coast call centre.
Many were persuaded to join by a simple Facebook ad click or cold call, followed by well-targeted sales tactics and a fateful decision to invest their nest egg in the schemes. Most of their money ultimately vanished.
New revelations into the explosive operation unmask two warring families at the centre of the network, whose corporate implosions mirrored a terrifying behind-the-scenes meltdown that tore apart the thriving enterprise.
For the first time, analysis of thousands of court and company documents pulls back the curtain on how this wealth-draining engine room operated.
Despite multiple company collapses, regulator scrutiny and ruined retirements, new companies with familiar names have sprung up in their place, luring new customers with the same promises of wealth and security. The Gold Coast operation was driven by the Pappas family – led by property developer Chris Pappas Sr, his son Chris Pappas Jr and daughter Isabella – and the Doumani family – Jack and his sons John and James.
From their well-equipped offices in Bundall – where the carpark shone with Bentleys and McLarens – they oversaw a highly profitable network of financial salespeople, known as lead generators, drawing investors from cities and towns throughout Australia for more than four years.
Sworn court documents expose the network’s staggering scale, revealing it took in roughly $400,000 a month from a four per cent upfront fee on super rollovers – equating to an estimated $10m in fresh retirement savings captured every month.
In an affidavit, Pappas Jr said the companies also took an ongoing two per cent annual fee generating $300,000 monthly – a revenue snapshot that implies a minimum of $180m in mum-and-dad funds under management.
But it all fell apart in 2024.
Pappas Jr’s affidavit was lodged as part of 2024 Supreme Court action launched by him and his sister Isabella, who successfully sought to wind up the companies they’d jointly operated with the Doumanis.
The billion-dollar collapses of the Shield and First Guardian funds, as well as the Pappas Sr-directed Global Capital Property Fund, have put a spotlight on “lead generation” – a business model widely used by so-called wealth advisory companies targeting the nation’s hefty superannuation kitty. Many who invested were persuaded by a Facebook ad offering a free super review or a competition to win a prize.
After they fill out a form from the post, a slick phone call from a friendly-sounding salesperson follows. Workers were encouraged to roll their retirement savings into self-managed super funds.
From there, the funds are funnelled into investments that are often high-risk and, in many cases, related parties of the lead generators or fund operators.
For the architects of the Gold Coast sales machine, operations that drew the attention of authorities were nothing new.
In 2024, Jack and John Doumani, along with Pappas Jr, put a long-running multimillion-dollar fraud case in the rearview.
The men had been charged in 2015 and accused of selling false betting products – but the charges were dropped after a disorganised prosecution caused oppressive court delays.
Pappas Jnr lived a fast-paced life in motorsport, plastering his race car with logos to promote his business ventures including now-collapsed firm WealthRite and his father’s company Point Bay Developments, which has since been the subject of multiple court actions to freeze its assets.
Pappas Jr had recovered from a fiery high-speed crash in 2022, when he and his future wife Krystle were pulled from the wreckage of his $330,000 McLaren supercar.
But the damage was more profound when the lucrative Pappas-Doumani partnership crashed and burned in March 2024.
In a sworn Supreme Court affidavit, filed as part of the winding up application, Pappas Jr said the relationship imploded after Jack Doumani accused Pappas Sr of taking money out of the shared business.
Doumani allegedly demanded full ownership of the wealth advisory network, threw office furniture, pinned Pappas Jr against a wall and threatened to “knock him out” if he didn’t sign it over. Pappas Jr alleged the intimidation followed him home.
In a recorded phone call on March 22, 2024, lodged as evidence in the Supreme Court, Jack Doumani allegedly told Pappas Jr – who at the time had a baby son – that he’d “f***ed with the wrong person”.
“Chris, baby or no baby, I’m telling you now, ok, it’s not a threat it’s a promise,” the transcript said.
“I’m gonna come to your place. I’ve been reasonable. I’ve been giving you every f***ing chance to come clean. I’m going to put a f***ing bullet in your head. Understand? I’ve lost all fucking respect you f***ing rat.” Pappas Jr claimed he was forced to hire private security.
One private security firm walked off the job, according to the court document, telling Pappas Jr it was simply “getting too dangerous” to protect them.
Doumani’s submissions in the case did not address the allegations of threatening behaviour.
The claims of violence didn’t stop there.
Pappas Jr survived a savage onslaught with a hammer and knives by masked men in an early morning raid on his waterfront mansion in August 2024.
While the attack was referenced in the Supreme Court matter, there is no suggestion anyone in the Doumani family was responsible or played any part in it.
Tweed man Joshua Timothy James Phillips is scheduled to be sentenced later this month for assaults occasioning bodily harm while armed/in company, among other charges related to the attack.
Following the explosive rift, eight companies linked to the families were pushed into liquidation, leaving thousands of clients and millions in debts in their wake.
The most recent liquidator reports lodged with ASIC suggest the companies still owe more $7m to creditors – but that does not include the tens of millions invested in the failed Global Capital fund, or untold investor money that flowed to the Shield Master Fund. Among the now-collapsed Gold Coast lead generation companies were Integral Wealth Group, Integral Advisory and WealthRite, which funnelled investor cash into property business Chiodo Corporation, according to a sworn affidavit from Pappas Jr.
ASIC is currently suing Chiodo Corporation director Paul Chiodo for allegedly breaching his director and officer duties over his alleged role in the Shield disaster, which drew in more than $500m from 5800 investors before its collapse.
Chiodo Corporation is named in the ASIC lawsuit as allegedly using investor funds to finance property including the JW Marriott Resort & Spa in Venice, Italy and the Ritz-Carton, Fiji.
Mr Chiodo is yet to file a defence in the matter.
The Gold Coast network initially operated under the financial licence of Melbourne-based United Global Capital, which was placed into voluntary liquidation in 2024 amid court action by the corporate regulator.
The Pappas-Doumani operation got its own financial services licence and began pointing money to a fund that was closer to home – the Global Capital Property Fund, which was directed by Pappas Sr, Brett Dickinson and banned UGC director Joel Hewish.
GCPF’s liquidators found the company invested around $93.8m into 14 projects, and a Federal Court judge found only one of them got off the ground.
The court case found that GCPF paid over $4.5m in fees to GCPF Management, a related entity also directed by Pappas Sr, Hewish and Dickinson.
Ipswich local Leisha Farrugia and her husband were juggling the demands of full-time jobs and school-aged kids when the phone calls started out of the blue, urging her to take advantage of a ‘free super check’.
On the third or fourth call, she relented, agreeing to an assessment from an adviser linked to United Global Capital.
The adviser encouraged her to pool the couple’s entire retirement savings – around $350,000 – into an SMSF that was invested in the Global Capital Property Fund.
“We thought we were safe, there were promises across the board,” Ms Farrugia said.
Ms Farrugia, who herself works in the finance sector, said it had left her feeling “ridiculously stupid”.
The Farrugias were able to claim against the government’s Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, which can pay up to $150,000 in compensation to those who have lodged a successful complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. The scheme is funded by a levy on financial services companies but is facing a shortfall of at least $170m to pay out more than 1500 claims that have been lodged.
